question: What is the universe made of?
blurb: Everything you can touch is built from a handful of particles held together by four forces, yet that ordinary matter is only about five percent of the cosmos. Follow the trail from atoms to quantum fields to the dark matter and dark energy that nobody has yet identified.

lessons.note: Protons, neutrons and electrons: the starting inventory of every object you have ever touched.
Quarks, leptons, antimatter and the three generations that make up the Standard Model.
The four forces and the boson messengers that carry them, including why quarks never appear alone.
What the Higgs field does, and why most of your mass actually comes from the strong force.
Why physicists stopped treating particles as tiny balls and started treating them as ripples in fields.
The Big Bang, the cosmic microwave background and inflation: where the ingredients came from.
How galaxy rotation and the cosmic web reveal matter that emits no light.
The accelerating expansion and dark energy, the largest and least understood part of the universe.

tours.title: Foundations of Quantum Mechanics
tours.status: Quantum mechanics predicts experiments with extraordinary accuracy, but there is still no agreement on what it says about reality: the main interpretations make the same predictions for all experiments done so far, and only collapse models are currently being tested directly.

stops.heading: The measurement problem
stops.html:
Quantum mechanics gives a system a wavefunction that evolves smoothly and deterministically under the Schrödinger equation. Left alone, an electron can be in a superposition of passing through two slits at once. Yet when you measure, you always get one definite result, with probabilities given by the Born rule.

The trouble is that measuring devices are made of atoms too. If the Schrödinger equation applies to everything, the apparatus should itself enter a superposition of showing both results, and so should you when you look at it. Schrödinger's cat, in 1935, was built to make this vivid. The textbook recipe simply adds a second rule, the collapse of the wavefunction on measurement, without saying what counts as a measurement or why ordinary physics stops applying. Each interpretation is a different answer to this gap.

stops.heading: Copenhagen and QBism: quantum states as tools
stops.html:
The Copenhagen interpretation, associated with Bohr and Heisenberg in the 1920s and 1930s, is less a single doctrine than a family of views. Its core is that physics must be described in terms of classical experimental arrangements, and that the wavefunction is a tool for predicting measurement outcomes rather than a picture of an underlying reality. Asking what the electron is doing between measurements is treated as a question without meaning.

QBism (Quantum Bayesianism), developed from the early 2000s by Christopher Fuchs, Rüdiger Schack and Carlton Caves, pushes this further. A quantum state represents one agent's degrees of belief about the results of their own future actions on the world. Collapse is simply that agent updating their beliefs on new experience, like a Bayesian gambler. Critics reply that both views avoid the measurement problem by declining to describe the world, rather than by solving it.

stops.heading: Many-Worlds: take the equation at its word
stops.html:
In his 1957 thesis, Hugh Everett proposed dropping collapse altogether. The universal wavefunction always obeys the Schrödinger equation. When you measure a superposition, you become entangled with it, and the combined state contains one branch in which you saw each outcome. Bryce DeWitt later popularised this as the Many-Worlds interpretation.

The theory of decoherence, developed from the 1970s, explains why the branches stop interfering: tiny interactions with the environment spread the superposition into countless untracked degrees of freedom, so each branch behaves as if classical. Everett's picture is economical in its laws but lavish in its worlds. Its hardest open issue is probability: if every outcome happens, what does it mean to say one outcome has a 90 percent chance? Proposed derivations of the Born rule from decision theory remain contested.

stops.heading: Pilot waves and objective collapse
stops.html:
Bohmian mechanics (the de Broglie-Bohm theory) keeps both a wave and real particles. Louis de Broglie proposed it in 1927 and David Bohm completed it in 1952. Particles always have definite positions and are guided by the wavefunction, which never collapses. The theory is deterministic, and it reproduces the standard statistical predictions if the initial positions are distributed according to the Born rule. The price is explicit non-locality: the motion of one particle can depend instantaneously on the positions of distant ones.

Objective collapse theories change the equations instead. In the GRW model (Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber, 1986), each particle has a tiny random chance of spontaneously localising, so rare for one particle that isolated atoms behave quantum mechanically, but amplified in a macroscopic object of some 10²³ particles so that superpositions of pointer positions die almost instantly. Roger Penrose and Lajos Diósi have proposed that gravity triggers the collapse.

stops.heading: Bell's theorem and the experiments
stops.html:
In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen argued that quantum mechanics must be incomplete, and that hidden variables could restore a local, definite reality. In 1964 John Bell proved that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce all the predictions of quantum mechanics: correlations between entangled particles measured far apart must obey an inequality that quantum theory violates.

John Clauser and Stuart Freedman made the first test in 1972. Alain Aspect's experiments in 1982 switched the measurement settings while the photons were in flight, closing an important loophole. In 2015 three groups, at Delft, Vienna and NIST, performed loophole-free tests that closed the detection and locality loopholes at once, and Anton Zeilinger's group pioneered entanglement-based quantum communication. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger. Quantum correlations violate Bell inequalities: any viable interpretation must give up locality or some assumption about definite outcomes or measurement choices.

stops.heading: Same predictions, different worlds
stops.html:
Copenhagen, QBism, Many-Worlds and Bohmian mechanics are designed to agree with standard quantum mechanics in every experiment done so far. Choosing between them currently rests on other grounds: simplicity, locality, what counts as an explanation, and how well each can be extended to relativity and quantum field theory, where Bohmian mechanics in particular faces difficulties.

Collapse models are different, because they are genuinely different physics. They predict that superpositions of large enough objects must fail, and that collapse should leave faint traces such as tiny spontaneous heating or radiation. Interference has been seen with molecules of about 2,000 atoms (Markus Arndt's group, 2019) without any sign of collapse, and a 2020 underground experiment at Gran Sasso ruled out the simplest parameter-free version of the Diósi-Penrose model. Larger interference experiments and tests with levitated particles keep squeezing the remaining parameter space. If collapse is found, the measurement problem becomes an experimental discovery; if not, the debate stays philosophical.

question: How did life begin and change?
blurb: Somewhere on the early Earth, chemistry became biology, and a single lineage of cells went on to produce every living thing. Explore the leading ideas about life's origin, the mechanisms that drive evolution, and the catastrophes that repeatedly reset the story.

lessons.note: Before asking how life began, you need a working answer to what life is, and the edge cases that break every definition.
Miller-Urey, the RNA world and metabolism-first: the rival routes from chemistry to biology.
Deep-sea vents, natural proton gradients and what we can infer about LUCA, the last universal common ancestor.
The cell as the basic unit of life: membrane, genome and the machinery every organism shares.
Darwin's insight and the evidence that heritable variation plus selection explains the diversity of life.
Selection, drift, gene flow and sexual selection: the engines that actually change populations.
The rare leaps, such as the eukaryotic cell and multicellularity, that reorganised how life is built.
The Big Five mass extinctions, and how disaster cleared the stage for new groups, including the mammals.

question: What is a mind?
blurb: Your brain is 86 billion or so neurons trading electrical and chemical signals, yet from the inside it feels like a single point of view. Philosophy, neuroscience and machine learning each attack the question of how matter gives rise to thought, and whether a machine could ever have a mind of its own.

lessons.note: Dualism, monism and property dualism: the classic positions on how mind relates to body.
Identity theory, functionalism and Searle's Chinese Room: is a mind defined by what it is made of or what it does?
Qualia and the hard problem: why explaining behaviour may not explain experience.
Intentionality, the way thoughts are about things, and whether content lives in the head or the world.
The neuron and the action potential: the physical signal underneath every thought.
How synapses strengthen and memories form, showing a mind that physically rewires itself.
What neuroscience can and cannot yet say about consciousness.
The Turing test, machine consciousness and panpsychism: where the debate goes when minds need not be human.

question: What can be computed and known?
blurb: In the 1930s Gödel and Turing proved that some true statements can never be proved and some questions can never be answered by any algorithm. Beyond those hard limits lie practical ones: problems that are solvable in principle but may take longer than the age of the universe.

lessons.note: Turing's imaginary machine and the Church-Turing thesis: a precise definition of what computing means.
The halting problem, Rice's theorem and incompleteness: questions no algorithm can ever answer.
Gödel's incompleteness theorems stated carefully, and what undecidable statements look like.
How incompleteness ended Hilbert's dream and what philosophers have made of it since.
Cantor's diagonal argument, the trick that sits underneath both Gödel's and Turing's results.
P, NP and NP-completeness: the gap between problems we can solve and problems we can only check.
Kolmogorov complexity: a measure of randomness that is itself uncomputable.
What quantum computers can and cannot add, and where BQP sits relative to P and NP.

tours.title: P vs NP
tours.status: Open since it was formalised in 1971 and one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems; most researchers believe P is not equal to NP, and three proven barrier theorems show that many familiar proof techniques cannot settle it.

stops.heading: Two classes of problems
stops.html:
Complexity theory sorts problems by how the work grows as the input grows. P is the class of yes-or-no problems a computer can solve in polynomial time: if the input has n symbols, the steps needed are bounded by something like n² or n³. Sorting a list, finding a shortest route on a map, and checking whether a number is prime (proved in P in 2002) all belong here.

NP is the class of problems where a proposed answer can be checked in polynomial time. Given a filled-in Sudoku, you verify it quickly. Given a claimed factorisation of a large number, you multiply and compare. Every problem in P is in NP, since if you can solve it fast you can certainly check it fast. The question is whether the reverse holds: does P equal NP?

stops.heading: Finding versus checking
stops.html:
Intuition says finding is harder than checking. Recognising a good proof is easier than writing one; spotting that a jigsaw is finished is easier than finishing it. For many NP problems the only known general methods amount to searching an exponential number of candidates, and 2ⁿ outruns any polynomial long before n reaches a few hundred.

But intuition is not a proof. Sometimes a clever idea collapses a search: linear programming looked hard until polynomial-time algorithms were found in 1979, and primality testing waited until 2002. P = NP would mean that every problem with quickly checkable answers has such a shortcut. Kurt Gödel saw the stakes early: in a 1956 letter to John von Neumann he asked, in effect, whether proofs of bounded length could be found mechanically in time roughly proportional to their length, and noted this would transform mathematics.

stops.heading: NP-completeness: the hardest problems in NP
stops.html:
In 1971 Stephen Cook proved that Boolean satisfiability (SAT: can you set the variables of a logical formula so that it comes out true?) is NP-complete. Every problem in NP can be translated into SAT in polynomial time, so a fast algorithm for SAT would give a fast algorithm for everything in NP. Leonid Levin found the same result independently in the Soviet Union, which is why it is called the Cook-Levin theorem.

In 1972 Richard Karp showed that 21 famous combinatorial problems are NP-complete too, including graph colouring, the clique problem, Hamiltonian cycle and integer programming. Thousands more have followed, from scheduling to protein folding models. They all stand or fall together: solve any one quickly and P = NP; prove any one needs superpolynomial time and P ≠ NP. Ladner showed in 1975 that if P ≠ NP, there are also problems strictly in between.

stops.heading: Why it matters
stops.html:
Much of modern cryptography assumes that some functions are easy to compute but hard to invert. If such one-way functions exist then P ≠ NP, so a proof that P = NP with a practical algorithm would break public-key cryptography, digital signatures and much of internet security. (Note the logic: P ≠ NP alone does not guarantee that cryptography is safe, since a problem can be hard in the worst case yet easy for typical instances. Factoring, used by RSA, is not known to be NP-complete.)

The optimistic side is just as dramatic. Logistics, chip design, drug discovery and many scheduling problems are NP-hard optimisation tasks, currently handled with heuristics that often work but carry no guarantees. A fast general algorithm would solve them exactly. It would also automate the search for mathematical proofs of any reasonable length.

stops.heading: Barriers that are themselves theorems
stops.html:
Part of what makes P vs NP remarkable is that researchers have proved why common approaches fail.

  • Relativization (Baker, Gill and Solovay, 1975): there are oracles, imaginary black boxes, relative to which P = NP, and others relative to which P ≠ NP. Any proof technique that works unchanged in the presence of any oracle, such as the diagonalisation used for the halting problem, cannot resolve the question.
  • Natural proofs (Razborov and Rudich, 1994): a broad family of circuit lower-bound arguments would, if they proved P ≠ NP, also yield a way to break pseudorandom generators that are widely believed secure.
  • Algebrization (Aaronson and Wigderson, 2008): the algebraic techniques behind results such as IP = PSPACE also fall short.

A proof must therefore be non-relativizing, non-natural and non-algebrizing all at once.

stops.heading: Where things stand
stops.html:
The question remains open. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, with a one million dollar prize. Claimed proofs appear regularly, in both directions, and none has survived expert scrutiny.

Most researchers believe P ≠ NP. In polls of theorists run by William Gasarch, the share holding that view grew from about 61 percent in 2002 to about 88 percent in 2019. The evidence is circumstantial: decades of failed attempts to find fast algorithms for thousands of NP-complete problems, across many unrelated fields.

Current programmes include circuit complexity, proof complexity and Ketan Mulmuley's geometric complexity theory, which recasts lower bounds as questions in algebraic geometry and representation theory. Even much weaker statements remain unproved: for general Boolean circuits, nobody has shown that any explicit NP problem needs more than a small constant times n gates.

question: Why do societies rise and fall?
blurb: Rome, the Mongols and the Bronze Age palace states all grew to dominate their worlds and then came apart. Historians, political scientists and economists offer rival explanations: institutions, climate, disease, overreach, revolt. Weigh them against the cases.

lessons.note: The first cities, writing and law codes: what a complex society needed in order to exist at all.
What makes an empire, with Rome, Han China and the Mauryas as the classic cases.
The crisis of the third century and the long debate over why the Western Roman Empire fell.
Drought, plague and the Little Ice Age: the case that climate helped topple societies.
The Mongol conquests and the Black Death, showing how connection brings both empire and pandemic.
Extractive versus inclusive institutions, and the argument that rules, not geography, decide who prospers.
State capacity and failed states: why building a working state is so hard and losing one so easy.
Skocpol, Tilly and Goldstone on when regimes break from within.

question: What is money and who controls it?
blurb: Money only works because everyone expects everyone else to accept it. Most of it today is created not by printing presses but by commercial banks making loans, while central banks and the global dollar system set the terms. Find out who holds the levers and what happens when trust breaks.

lessons.note: The functions of money, from commodity coins to fiat currency, and money as a social convention.
Money, credit and banking in pre-modern economies: the long history behind today's system.
How commercial banks create new money when they lend, and what limits them.
Central banks: open market operations, lender of last resort and the fight over independence.
Bank runs and the 2008 crisis: what happens when confidence in money-like claims fails.
Reserve currencies, the petrodollar and the dollar's exorbitant privilege.
Monetary power as statecraft: sanctions and the weaponisation of the financial system.
Stablecoins and the Terra collapse: private attempts to issue money, and how they break.

question: How does language shape thought?
blurb: Every human society has language, and roughly seven thousand languages carve up the world in strikingly different ways. Do the categories your language provides change how you perceive and remember, or is there a shared human mind beneath them all? Linguistics offers evidence on both sides.

lessons.note: Sense, reference and prototype categories, plus the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis and its colour-term evidence.
Chomsky's generative grammar: the case for a universal, innate language faculty.
Ergative and topic-prominent languages, and the poverty-of-the-stimulus debate.
Isolating, agglutinative and fusional languages, and noun-class systems that force speakers to sort the world.
Tone and intonation: languages in which pitch changes the meaning of a word.
How the way you speak signals class, gender and identity, and how prestige shapes choices.
Language families and the comparative method: how languages diverge from a common ancestor.
Language death and revival: what is lost when a language disappears.

question: What is a good life?
blurb: Aristotle said the good life is flourishing through virtue, the utilitarians said it is happiness, the Buddha located it in freedom from craving, and the existentialists said you must invent the answer yourself. Compare the great traditions and test them against hard cases.

lessons.note: What ethics is, whether moral facts exist, and Hume's gap between is and ought.
Aristotle's eudaimonia and the doctrine of the mean: the good life as a life of flourishing.
Bentham and Mill: the good life measured in happiness, and the objections that dog it.
Kant's categorical imperative: duty and respect for persons, whatever the consequences.
Confucius and the junzi: a good life lived through relationships, ritual and self-cultivation.
The Four Noble Truths and non-self: suffering, craving and the way out.
Camus's absurd and Beauvoir's ambiguity: meaning made rather than found.
Trolley problems, moral luck and moral uncertainty: where the neat theories meet real choices.

question: What are the great unsolved problems?
blurb: Some questions have resisted the best minds for more than a century. Some are precise enough that a million-dollar prize awaits the answer; others are so open that nobody is sure what an answer would look like. Here is where current knowledge runs out.

lessons.note: Primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic: the raw material of the oldest open problems.
Twin primes, Goldbach and the Riemann Hypothesis: famous conjectures that are easy to state and unproved.
The prime number theorem and the zeta function, the tools needed to understand the Riemann Hypothesis.
P versus NP, the central open question of computer science.
What the Standard Model cannot explain: dark matter, neutrino masses, gravity and unification.
The open questions of cosmology, and the new messengers being used to probe them.
The hard problem of consciousness: an open question so deep there is no agreed method for attacking it.
The Drake equation and Fermi's paradox: are we alone, and why is the sky so quiet?

tours.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
tours.status: Unproved since 1859 and one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems: every zero checked so far lies on the critical line, and the best theorems put over 40 percent of all zeros there, but nobody can show that all of them do.

stops.heading: Counting the primes
stops.html:
The primes look scattered at random: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, then a gap, then 17 and 19. Yet if you stop asking where the next prime is and ask how many primes lie below x, a pattern appears. Call that count π(x). As a teenager, Gauss guessed that primes near x have density about 1/ln x, so π(x) should be close to x/ln x, or better, to the logarithmic integral li(x).

That guess became the Prime Number Theorem, proved independently by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin in 1896. It says the ratio of π(x) to x/ln x tends to 1. But a ratio tending to 1 says nothing about how large the leftover error is. The Riemann Hypothesis is, at heart, a precise claim about that error: how far the primes can stray from their average behaviour.

stops.heading: Euler's bridge and Riemann's continuation
stops.html:
In 1737 Euler noticed that the sum 1 + 1/2ˢ + 1/3ˢ + ... equals a product over all primes p of 1/(1 − p⁻ˢ). This Euler product is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic in disguise, and it ties the primes to a smooth function, now called the zeta function ζ(s).

The sum only converges when the real part of s is greater than 1. In his only paper on number theory (1859), Riemann let s be a complex number and showed that ζ extends to the whole complex plane, apart from a single pole at s = 1. This is analytic continuation: there is exactly one smooth (holomorphic) way to extend the function, so the extension is not a choice but a discovery. Riemann also found a functional equation linking ζ(s) to ζ(1 − s), a mirror symmetry about the line Re(s) = 1/2.

stops.heading: The critical line
stops.html:
The extended zeta function has two kinds of zeros. The trivial zeros sit at −2, −4, −6 and so on, and are well understood. All the others, the non-trivial zeros, lie inside the critical strip where the real part of s is between 0 and 1. They come in symmetric pairs, reflected across the line Re(s) = 1/2.

Riemann computed the first few, found them sitting exactly on that line, and wrote that it was "very probable" all of them do. That remark is the Riemann Hypothesis: every non-trivial zero has real part exactly 1/2. Riemann also sketched an explicit formula expressing the prime count as a main term minus a sum of waves, one for each zero. The zeros are the frequencies of the primes, so their positions control how the primes wobble around their average.

stops.heading: Ten trillion zeros on the line
stops.html:
The numerical evidence is overwhelming. Computations by Xavier Gourdon and Patrick Demichel in 2004 checked the first ten trillion (10¹³) non-trivial zeros, and every one lies on the critical line. Andrew Odlyzko computed zeros far higher up, near the 10²⁰th, and found them on the line too.

Odlyzko's data showed something stranger. The spacings between neighbouring zeros follow the same statistics as the eigenvalues of large random Hermitian matrices, the ensemble physicists use to model energy levels of heavy nuclei. Hugh Montgomery had predicted this pair correlation in 1973, and Freeman Dyson recognised the formula over tea. It hints that the zeros might be the energy levels of some unknown quantum system, an idea known as the Hilbert-Pólya approach.

Numbers, however many, are not a proof. In number theory, patterns have held for astronomically large ranges and then failed.

stops.heading: What a proof would give you
stops.html:
In 1901 Helge von Koch showed that the Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to a sharp error term: π(x) differs from li(x) by at most a constant times √x · ln x. In plain terms, the primes would be as evenly spread as randomness could possibly allow. Without the hypothesis, the best proven error bounds are far weaker.

Hundreds of published theorems begin "Assume the Riemann Hypothesis" or its generalisation to other L-functions. They cover the size of gaps between consecutive primes, the speed of deterministic primality tests (the Miller test runs in polynomial time if the generalised hypothesis holds), and the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions. A proof would turn all of these conditional results into theorems at a stroke. A counterexample, a single zero off the line, would bring many of them down.

stops.heading: Partial results and why it is hard
stops.html:
Progress has come in pieces. In 1914 Hardy proved that infinitely many zeros lie on the line. In 1942 Atle Selberg showed that a positive proportion do. Norman Levinson raised that to at least one third in 1974, and Brian Conrey to more than two fifths in 1989. Later refinements have nudged the figure only slightly higher. In 2024 Larry Guth and James Maynard improved a bound on how many zeros can lie far from the line, beating an estimate of Ingham that had stood since 1940.

The difficulty is that every known method controls zeros on average, while the hypothesis is a statement about every single one. There is also no proof that the zeros must avoid any fixed strip close to Re(s) = 1, only regions that thin out as you climb. Hilbert put the problem on his 1900 list, and in 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute offered one million dollars for its solution. It remains open.
